notes.summary: Sampling theory is about studying a part of a population to learn about the whole. Paper 2 asks about census versus sample surveys, sampling and non-sampling errors, the main sampling methods (simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster, and non-random methods), how to allocate a sample to strata, and the standard error of a mean or proportion, with or without the finite population correction.

concepts.title: Basic terms
concepts.body:
• Population (universe): every unit we want to study. Its size is N.
  • Sample: the part actually studied. Its size is n. Sampling fraction f = n/N.
  • Sampling frame: the list (or map) of units from which the sample is drawn, such as a voter list.
  • Sampling unit: the unit that is selected (a household, a village, a field).
  • Parameter: a value describing the population (μ, σ, P). Statistic: a value worked out from the sample (x̄, s, p).
  • Sampling distribution: the distribution of a statistic over all possible samples. Its SD is the standard error.

concepts.title: Census and sample survey
concepts.body:
Census (complete enumeration)Sample survey
Every unit is studiedOnly selected units are studied
Costly and slowCheaper and faster
No sampling errorHas sampling error, which can be measured
Large non-sampling errors (more staff, less training)Fewer non-sampling errors, better-trained staff
Needed when data on every unit is required, or the population is smallThe only choice when testing destroys the item (life of bulbs, crash tests) or the population is infinite

India's Population Census (every 10 years) is a census; NSS (National Sample Survey) rounds are sample surveys.

concepts.title: Sampling and non-sampling errors
concepts.body:
• Sampling error: the difference between a statistic and the parameter that arises only because a part is studied. It is zero in a census and falls as n grows (roughly like 1/√n).
  • Non-sampling error: comes from everything else, and is present in both census and sample surveys. Sources: faulty questionnaire, interviewer bias, wrong answers, non-response, incomplete frame (coverage error), mistakes in coding, tabulation and printing. It tends to grow as the size of the enquiry grows.
  • Biased errors push results one way and do not cancel out; unbiased (random) errors tend to cancel in large samples.

concepts.title: Sampling methods
concepts.body:
Probability (random) methodsNon-probability methods
Simple random sampling (lottery, random number table)Judgement (purposive) sampling: chosen by the investigator's judgement
Stratified random samplingQuota sampling: interviewers fill fixed quotas for each group
Systematic samplingConvenience sampling: whoever is easy to reach
Cluster sampling, multistage samplingSnowball sampling: each respondent refers others

In a probability method every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, so the sampling error can be measured. Non-probability methods do not allow this.

concepts.title: Simple random sampling
concepts.body:
• Every unit (and every possible sample of size n) has the same chance of selection.
  • SRSWR (with replacement): a unit may be picked again. Ordered samples = Nn.
  • SRSWOR (without replacement): no repeats. Possible samples = NCn, each with probability 1/NCn.
  • Chance that a particular unit is in an SRSWOR sample = n/N.
  • The sample mean ȳ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean in both cases.
Var(ȳ)
SRSWRσ²/n
SRSWOR(N − n)/(N − 1) × σ²/n = (1 − f) S²/n, where S² = Nσ²/(N − 1)

So SRSWOR is more precise than SRSWR for the same n. Example: N = 6, n = 2 gives 15 samples without replacement and 36 ordered samples with replacement.

concepts.title: Stratified random sampling
concepts.body:
• Divide the population into non-overlapping strata that are homogeneous within and different from each other, then take an SRS from each.
  • Gives more precise estimates than SRS when strata differ, and gives results for each stratum.
AllocationRule
Equalni = n/k
Proportional (Bowley)ni = n × Ni/N
Optimum (Neyman)ni = n × NiSi / ΣNiSi
Optimum with costni ∝ NiSi/√ci

Usually Var(Neyman) ≤ Var(proportional) ≤ Var(SRS).

concepts.title: Systematic and cluster sampling
concepts.body:
• Systematic: interval k = N/n. Pick a random start r between 1 and k, then take r, r + k, r + 2k, … Example: N = 500, n = 25, k = 20; start 7 gives 7, 27, 47, 67, 87, …
  • Easy and spreads the sample over the list, but can go badly wrong if the list has a pattern that repeats every k units (periodicity).
  • When N is not a multiple of n, circular systematic sampling is used.
  • Cluster: divide the population into groups (clusters) that are each mixed inside (heterogeneous), pick some clusters at random and study every unit in them. Cheap when units are spread out; no full list of units is needed.
  • Multistage: sample districts, then villages in them, then households. Area sampling uses map areas as clusters.

concepts.title: Standard error
concepts.body:
StatisticStandard error
Meanσ/√n
Mean, finite population without replacementσ/√n × √((N − n)/(N − 1))
Proportion√(PQ/n)
Difference of two means√(σ1²/n1 + σ2²/n2)
Difference of two proportions√(P1Q1/n1 + P2Q2/n2)
SD (large sample)σ/√(2n)
  • SE is proportional to 1/√n: to halve the SE, make n four times as big.
  • The correction √((N − n)/(N − 1)) is called the finite population correction (fpc). It is close to 1 and is usually ignored when n/N is below about 5%.
  • Sample size for a proportion with margin e: n = z²pq/e². For 95% (z = 1.96), p = 0.5, e = 0.05: n = 384.16, so take 385.

varieties.name: Census, sample survey and errors
varieties.how: Sampling error exists only because a part is studied; non-sampling error (non-response, bias, processing mistakes) can occur in both.

example.q: Which type of error can occur even in a complete census?
steps: A census studies every unit, so there is no sampling error.
Errors from wrong answers, non-response and tabulation can still occur.

varieties.name: Sampling methods
varieties.how: Match the description: homogeneous groups and sample from each is stratified; every k-th unit is systematic; whole groups chosen is cluster; quotas or judgement means non-random.

example.q: A population is divided into groups that are alike within, and a random sample is taken from every group. This is:
steps: Groups alike within (homogeneous) with a sample from each group.
This is the definition of stratified random sampling.
In cluster sampling only some groups are picked, and they are mixed inside.

varieties.name: Simple random sampling counts
varieties.how: Without replacement: <sup>N</sup>C<sub>n</sub> samples, inclusion chance n/N. With replacement: N<sup>n</sup> ordered samples.

example.q: From a population of 6 units, samples of size 2 are drawn by SRSWOR. How many samples are possible, and what is the chance that a given unit is included?

varieties.name: Systematic sampling
varieties.how: k = N/n. With random start r, the selected units are r, r + k, r + 2k, …, so the i-th unit is r + (i − 1)k.

example.q: A systematic sample of 25 is drawn from 500 units. The random start is 7. What is the 5th unit selected?

varieties.name: Allocation in stratified sampling
varieties.how: Proportional: n<sub>i</sub> ∝ N<sub>i</sub>. Neyman: n<sub>i</sub> ∝ N<sub>i</sub>S<sub>i</sub>. Check that the parts add to n.

example.q: Two strata: N<sub>1</sub> = 400, S<sub>1</sub> = 10; N<sub>2</sub> = 600, S<sub>2</sub> = 5. A sample of 70 is allocated by Neyman allocation. Find n<sub>1</sub> and n<sub>2</sub>.

varieties.name: Standard error
varieties.how: SE of mean = σ/√n, times √((N − n)/(N − 1)) for a finite population sampled without replacement. SE of proportion = √(pq/n).

example.q: A population of 500 has SD 20. A sample of 100 is drawn without replacement. Find the standard error of the mean.

tips: Stratified: homogeneous within strata. Cluster: heterogeneous within clusters. They are opposites.
Quota, judgement, convenience and snowball are the non-random methods.
To cut the standard error by a factor of m, multiply the sample size by m².
Neyman allocation gives a bigger sample to strata that are larger or more variable.
If n/N is small (under 5%), ignore the finite population correction.
Destructive testing (life of bulbs, crackers) can only be done by sampling.
traps: A census has no sampling error, but it does have non-sampling errors.
Increasing the sample size reduces sampling error, not non-sampling error.
Systematic sampling interval is N/n, not n/N.
SE of proportion uses pq/n under the square root; do not forget the square root.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NON-random sampling method?
questions.solution: In quota sampling the interviewer chooses units by his own judgment within fixed quotas, so units do not have a known chance of selection. The others are probability methods.

questions.q: A systematic sample of 60 units is to be drawn from a list of 1,200 units. The sampling interval k is:
questions.solution: k = N/n = 1200/60 = 20. After a random start between 1 and 20, every 20th unit is taken.

questions.q: A population has SD 12. The standard error of the mean for a random sample of size 36 is:
A population has two strata of sizes 600 and 400. A sample of 50 is taken with proportional allocation. The sample sizes from the two strata are:
In a sample of 96 people, 40% are found to be smokers. The standard error of the sample proportion is:
A sample of size 100 gives a certain standard error of the mean. To reduce this standard error to half, the sample size must be:
questions.solution:
SE ∝ 1/√n. Halving SE needs √n to double, i.e. n to become 4 times.
New n = 4 × 100 = 400.
